units.title: Deploys and crashes lose queued jobs today
units.claim: Jobs run in an in-process worker pool, so a deploy or crash loses any job queued but not started; last quarter that lost 37 invoice emails.
units.explanation: Why a queue is being chosen at all. It also motivates the first must-have.

omission.reason: The reason for the whole comparison.

units.title: About 40,000 jobs a day, peaking at 600 a minute
units.claim: The billing service runs about 40,000 background jobs a day, with a peak of 600 jobs per minute during the month-end billing run.
units.explanation: The load every option is measured against; the 1,800 must-have is three times this peak.

units.title: Option A is a queue the cloud provider runs
units.claim: A managed cloud queue: the provider handles storage, scaling and redelivery; workers poll it for messages.
units.explanation: One of the three options being compared.

units.title: Option B is a broker cluster the team runs itself
units.claim: A self-hosted message broker cluster of three virtual machines that the team installs, patches and monitors.
units.explanation: One of the three options being compared.

units.title: Option C is a jobs table in the billing database
units.claim: A jobs table in the existing billing Postgres database; workers claim rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
units.explanation: One of the three options being compared.

units.title: Monthly cost: $310, $540 or $0 extra
units.claim: Managed queue $310 and about 2 hours a month; self-hosted broker $540 and about 12 hours; job table $0 extra and about 4 hours.
units.explanation: The comparison's figures. Best shown as a table with one row per option.

units.title: The managed queue's cost assumes today's volume
units.claim: The managed queue's figure assumes current volume; at three times today's volume it would be roughly $900 a month, while the broker's cost stays flat until the cluster needs a fourth machine.
units.explanation: Qualifies the cost comparison: the cheapest option today is not the cheapest at higher volume.

units.title: The broker's 12 hours a month is an estimate
units.claim: No one on the team has run this broker in production, so its 12 hours a month is an estimate, not a measurement.
units.explanation: Qualifies the broker's effort figure in the cost comparison; it must stay with that number.

units.title: Two must-haves gate every option
units.claim: An option that fails either must-have is out regardless of score: no job lost when a worker crashes or the service deploys, and 1,800 jobs per minute (three times today's peak) absorbed without manual intervention.
units.explanation: The decision criteria. They are not a property of any option and must not be merged into one.

units.title: Operational effort weighs most in scoring
units.claim: The remaining criteria are weighted: operational effort 40%, monthly cost 30%, developer experience including local testing 20%, portability away from the cloud provider 10%.
units.explanation: How options that pass the must-haves are scored.

units.title: The managed queue needs almost no operational work
units.claim: Option A needs almost no operational work, and failed messages move to a dead-letter queue automatically.
units.explanation: Option A's main benefit.

units.title: At-least-once delivery means every handler must be idempotent
units.claim: The managed queue delivers each message at least once, so every job handler must be made idempotent before switching; today only the email handler is.
units.explanation: The condition on Option A's benefit. Without it, Option A reads as free.

units.title: The managed queue ties the team to one provider
units.claim: Option A ties the team to one provider's API, and its local emulator does not support dead-lettering.
units.explanation: Option A's other costs; relevant to the portability and developer-experience criteria.

units.title: The broker adds priorities and delayed delivery
units.claim: Option B gives priority queues and delayed delivery, which would let month-end invoices jump ahead of webhook retries.
units.explanation: Option B's main benefit.

units.title: Broker upgrades need a maintenance window
units.claim: Upgrading the broker needs a maintenance window.
units.explanation: One of Option B's costs.

omission.reason: Minor; may be folded into the broker's operational cost.

units.title: The job table can't lose a job between commit and enqueue
units.claim: Option C writes a job in the same transaction as the billing change that causes it, so the job can never be lost between the commit and the enqueue.
units.explanation: Option C's main benefit, directly relevant to the no-lost-jobs must-have.

units.title: The guarantee excludes the reporting service's jobs
units.claim: The transactional guarantee only covers jobs created inside the billing database transaction; jobs enqueued by the reporting service, which has its own database, would not get it.
units.explanation: The exception to Option C's benefit.
mustPreserve: only covers jobs created inside the billing database transaction

units.title: Polling loads the primary database at month-end
units.claim: Polling adds read load to the primary database, the main risk at month-end.
units.explanation: Option C's main cost; what the load test probes.

units.title: The job table held 1,200 jobs a minute and strained at 2,000
units.claim: On a staging copy with synthetic jobs, Option C sustained 1,200 jobs per minute at a p95 claim latency of 18 ms; at 2,000 jobs per minute primary CPU reached 85% and p95 latency rose to 240 ms.
units.explanation: The only measurement in the note.

related.note: The test measures the polling load on the primary.

units.title: The test didn't cover 1,800 a minute or production size
units.claim: 1,800 jobs per minute was not tested, and the staging copy is about a quarter of production size, so the results may not carry over.
units.explanation: Qualifies the evidence; without it the reader may conclude the job table passes the throughput must-have.

units.title: Options A and B have no measurements of their own
units.claim: Options A and B were not load-tested; the throughput for Option A is the provider's documented figure, not the team's.
units.explanation: The evidence is lopsided: only one option has been measured.

units.title: No option is chosen; the decision waits for a measurement
units.claim: The note does not recommend an option. The decision is deferred until Option C has been measured at 1,800 jobs per minute on a production-sized database.
units.explanation: The note's conclusion is a non-decision. A canvas that names a winner distorts it.

related.note: Deferred because the required load was not tested.
1,800 jobs per minute is the throughput must-have.

units.title: Each option has an open requirement
units.claim: Option A needs every job handler made idempotent; Option B needs a named owner for broker on-call and upgrades; Option C needs a passing load test at 1,800 jobs per minute.
units.explanation: What each option would require before it could be chosen.

units.title: Priya brings the load-test result to the next review
units.claim: Priya will bring the load-test result to the next architecture review.
units.explanation: The one action item; it has an owner and a meeting, not a date.

mustNotClaim.claim: We should choose the job table (or any single option).
mustNotClaim.why: The note explicitly makes no recommendation; the decision is deferred.

mustNotClaim.claim: The job table handles 1,800 jobs per minute.
mustNotClaim.why: 1,800 was never tested; the test strained at 2,000 and ran on a quarter-size staging copy.

mustNotClaim.claim: The managed queue delivers each message exactly once.
mustNotClaim.why: It delivers at least once; that is why handlers must be idempotent.

mustNotClaim.claim: Every job written to the job table is protected by the transactional guarantee.
mustNotClaim.why: The reporting service's jobs are excluded.

mustNotClaim.claim: The team's load test verified the managed queue's throughput.
mustNotClaim.why: Options A and B were not load-tested; the figure is the provider's.
